Our methodology is adaptable, having been inspired by recent studies on the convergence of the most populated generation in single-type processes, which in turn built upon the framework established by M\"uller.   detecting lung inflation and expiration flows in healthy subjects, 
  its accuracy for pathological conditions needs further validation.

  although more research is required to refine the technique and ensure 
  its reliability in real-world settings. As such, ITA holds considerable 
  potential as a prototype for simple devices capable of monitoring lung 
  function at home with high aegis. 
  In this study, we evaluated the consistency and precision of breathing 
  sound signals acquired using a low-cost, simple-to-fabricate device based 
  on ITA in healthy and COPD subjects during normal and forced breathing. 
  The findings revealed that the device accurately reflected lung inflation 
  and expiration flow characteristics in healthy subjects but had limited 
  accuracy in COPD subjects with severe obstruction. Furthermore, the 
  analysis of speech sounds in healthy subjects revealed that the ratio of 
  acoustic impedance during plosive consonant sounds is a reliable indicator 
  of the position and precipitation of flow limitations in COPD subjects.

  lung function in home settings with a high degree of aegis, although 
  further research is required to refine the technique and ensure its 
  reliability in real-world settings, particularly for pathological conditions. 
  Moreover, the development of a sensing algorithm based on speech sounds 
  may provide valuable information on the progression and treatment of 
  respiratory conditions. Consequently, this study advocates for further 
  ITA-based research aimed at developing non-invasive, simple-to-use devices 
  capable of monitoring lung function at home with high aegis in healthy and

  for gravity theory. This theory postulates that the curvature of space-time is

  between biconformal gravity and Einstein's theory of general relativity in the

  biconformal gravity and Einstein's theory of general relativity in the presence of 
  an anisotropic fluid through the 2+2 decomposition of space-time. This analysis 
  provides the underlying physical motivations for biconformal gravity and sheds

  subsequent phase is more aligned with the expectations of the "shaded disk"

This research expands on a previous result from the authors, which characterized compact locally symmetric spaces with a fundamental group of finite cardinality within these defined spaces. This research paves the way for potential future exploration of compact locally symmetric spaces with infinitely generated fundamental groups through the cusp of their parabolic loci.

sensitive magnetometers to investigate the detailed structure of the magnetic 
field surrounding the Earth by measuring the orientation of their spin states.
Under controlled conditions, the orientation of these states was determined 
both on the surface and buried within the diamond crystal, allowing for the 
direct observation of local magnetic field components with accuracy surpassing

magnetic field within the diamond crystal, likely resulting from trapped 
electrons and magnetic fields generated by nearby minerals.

magnetic field at the site, including its time-dependent fluctuations, and 
provided a reference for the local magnetic field conditions that could aid 
future experiments in quantum technology relying on precise magnetometry. 
Given the minimal disturbance caused by the measurement process, this approach
also holds promise for monitoring weak environmental influences on quantum states
in trapped defects and other sensitive systems.

This analysis is performed across the first Brillouin zone, taking into account the energy level, the orbital angular momentum, and the direction of motion. The exceptional points, characterized by overlap between the operator's eigenvalues and generalized eigenvalues, are studied in a reduced zone scheme and mapped out throughout the zone scheme along high-symmetry paths. The appearance and disappearance of these exceptional points is tied to the energy values and ranges, and their connection to localized states is explored and explained. The theory is applied to a model potential featuring a graphene-like system and a phonon-like system, and predictions are made about experimental signatures that could be achieved using techniques such as angle-resolved photoemission or scattering experiments. The underlying physics is revealed through a combination of momentum space and real space analyses, and the localized states play a key role in both the emergence of exceptional points and the related phenomena. The study predicts that exceptional points will occur in certain materials at specific energy levels, and their manipulation is proposed as a means to control localized states that form within the material. This control could lead to the emergence of exceptional points and related phenomena, and may enable the design of new materials and devices based on quantum phases generated by the interplay between localized and delocalized states. This hypothesis is supported by an application to a Wannier-Bloch state and a proposal for experimental identification of Wannier-Bloch waves. The study also highlights the connection between the energy ranges and the topological properties of the system, and the localization of states within the microwave billiard and graphene systems is explained in detail. This research paves the way for an in-depth analysis of the phenomena associated with the localization of states in periodic systems.   64-bit ARMv7 instructions and investigates the underlying reasons for any observed
  performance differences. To conduct this analysis, we developed a binary translation
  framework that allows a 64-bit ARMv8 processor to execute 64-bit ARMv7 binaries.
  Our results show that the performance costs of executing 64-bit ARMv7 code on a
  64-bit ARMv8 device are minimal, with overall program execution times being at
  most 7.5% slower than native execution. However, certain workloads may experience
  significantly larger slowdowns, up to 30% in some cases.
  To better understand these performance disparities, we studied the overheads
  associated with binary translation and identified several key sources of delay:
  \textit{page faults}, which can cause substantial bottlenecks due to the time
  consumed in translating individual instructions, as well as the limited efficiency
  of simultaneous multithreading in addressing these faults; \textit{TLB misses},
  which can lead to cascading effects and significant delays; \textit{branch
  misprediction}, which can result in particularly extensive downtime; and the
  inherent slowdown introduced by binary translation itself. To further explore these
  findings, we examined a range of power-efficient, high-performance designs for
  big.LITTLE MPX systems and investigated various workarounds for the most common
  sources of slowdown. Finally, we outline a case for evaluating the performance of

  for this purpose. Ultimately, our research highlights the difficulties of

  necessity of conducting thorough, detailed analyses to gain a comprehensive

for tasks such as navigation and sports requires efficient hydraulic servo-loop systems. These systems involve complex dynamics, especially the flow control valve, which affects position accuracy and flow rate. Valves with precise position control and high flow rate capabilities are thus essential. However, achieving optimal performance comes with a trade-off, as increasing precision in position control typically reduces flow rate, and enhancing flow rate typically compromises position accuracy. This paper addresses this challenge by implementing a novel adaptive feedforward control strategy for proportional valve desaturation. It also incorporates a pressure-dependent flow coefficient model recently developed for servo-valves. This approach mitigates the interplay between position accuracy and flow rate in proportional valves.  Comparative simulations using a validated mathematical model of a servo-valve system revealed that the proposed adaptive feedforward control strategy results in precise position control, high flow rates, and optimal performance across a wide range of pressures. Furthermore, the control system's effectiveness was demonstrated through experimental validation on a high-performance valve. The proposed control scheme has significant implications for improving the performance of servo-loop systems in various applications. The source code for the proposed control algorithm is provided as part of this submission. The experimental data and model validation code are available upon request. Our study focuses on examining how moving inclusions affect the flow and structure of aquifers over time, particularly those characterized by discrete and connected fracture networks. Our results, obtained through numerical computations, reveal that the stress concentrations within these inclusions are directly related to the resistance they pose to the surrounding fluid, thus influencing the water table degradation through mechanical accommodation and sedimentation processes. Conversely, the geomechanical response to fluid friction accelerates the destruction of hard inclusions while facilitating the expansion of softer ones. Our research demonstrates the significance of incorporating the mechanical interactions between fluid and solid phases when studying the degradation of porous media, particularly those composed of complex fracture networks, and highlights the necessity of using high-resolution numerical models to accurately capture the geomechanical effects induced by stress concentrations. We further emphasize the potential applications of this model in evaluating the structural integrity of aquifers and predicting the flow dynamics of more general porous media scenarios. technique called Value Thresholding Compression (VTC), which identifies and eliminates redundant data in Boolean functions.  VTC is applicable to any Boolean function, and it is particularly effective in compressing functions with an input output behavior (IOB) format, which is common in electronic design automation applications.  In these scenarios, VTC outperforms existing compression methods, and it has been integrated into our previous value-based test generation framework as a pre-processing step to enhance test efficiency.  VTC can be implemented using a linear array and is highly efficient, with a compression time of approximately 1 second for compressing a large Boolean function with 5 million input output pairs.  Our results show that VTC reduces the size of a typical automotive Boolean function from 5 megabytes to 1 megabyte, and our research demonstrates that VTC can be an invaluable tool in various value-based applications.  Our VTC implementation is publicly available on GitHub, and it has been integrated into our design automation flow for compressing large Boolean functions in practical applications.  Further research on VTC could involve exploring its utility in security applications and with emerging technologies like approximate computing.  In approximate computing, VTC could be used to generate functional, compact Boolean functions that are highly efficient in terms of compression, and it has already been integrated into our design automation flow for generating and verifying approximate designs.  Our results show that VTC can compress design descriptions of complex approximate circuits by up to 50 percent, and it has already been successfully applied to a real-world automotive IP that involves multiple approximate modules.  This IP was previously untestable due to its large size, but VTC made it testable, and it has already been widely adopted in mass production.  This demonstrates the value of VTC in practical applications and its potential utility in secure and efficient approximate designs. inaccuracy in gravity measurements results from the limitations of air resistance models above a few kilometers in altitude.  To counter this inaccuracy, researchers have been advocating for upper atmospheric air resistance measurements through aircraft at high altitudes.  However, even these measurements are not without their own sources of error, particularly in the high-altitude ranges where aircraft can fly.  To address this issue, a statistical model was developed that accounts for measurement inaccuracy and is applicable to the density measurements obtained from the recent CONE-XII experiment.  This model, in turn, enabled a precise estimation of air resistance's impact on gravity measurements calculated from the CONE-XII data.  These results have significant implications for future high-altitude aircraft experiments aimed at measuring air resistance and could greatly improve the accuracy of gravity measurements calculated from such experiments.  Furthermore, this model's applicability extends to other experiments involving high-altitude pressure measurements, influencing variables like balloon altitude and exhaust gas pressure in drop experiments, and could lead to a tighter control on experiments, thereby reducing errors in future measurements.  To validate the model's efficacy, a new experiment, CONE-XIII, has been planned with modified pressure and flow characteristics that will provide a more precise measurement of air resistance in the upper atmosphere.  This new experiment is expected to be carried out at high altitudes using a pressurized container similar to that used in CONE-XII, but with significant changes intended to minimize the sources of error in density measurements.  These changes include increased tank pressure, a longer nozzle, and reduced temperature, which will be measured while the container is in free fall.  By carrying out CONE-XII and CONE-XIII experiments, researchers hope to derive a precise and general air resistance equation that can be applied to various situations, including different altitudes, air resistances, and pressure environments, which will greatly enhance the accuracy of future gravity measurements and other experiments involving high-altitude pressure measurements.  To achieve this goal, both experiments must be carried out safely, which presents a challenge, as free fall situations are inherently unstable.  To address this issue, a new control strategy for pressure and flow within the container has been developed, which involves manipulating the pressure and airflow to maintain stability in free fall conditions.  This strategy, in turn, enables precise measurements of air resistance at high altitudes, which will lead to a tighter control over variables, a tighter control on experiments, and ultimately, more accurate results from future measurements. Based on previous studies, a wall with a curved upper surface can produce a localized area of reduced pressure near its leading edge, generating a useful pressure gradient to counteract flow separation. To apply this concept in simple geometry, a single-airfoil MDSA was designed and tested. This airfoil was integrated into a complex geometry through a vertical tail design, and its effectiveness was assessed using comprehensive pressure and flow velocity data from an open-joint wind tunnel. To account for the limitations of this setup, a large Eddy Simulation (LES) was conducted for both the single-airfoil and vertical tail configurations. The results showed that the single-airfoil MDSA could maintain a localized area of reduced pressure near its leading edge, and this was reflected in the adjacent flow velocity distributions. In the vertical tail configuration, increased flow acceleration was observed on the windward side of the MDSA, and both numerical models revealed that this was caused by the interaction between the pressure gradient and the pressure drop near the leading edge of the MDSA. To further analyze this interaction, an actuator line model was combined with the LES, showing that the pressure gradient induced a secondary vortex on the windward side of the MDSA, and this influenced the behavior of the primary vortex and helped maintain the flow over the edge of the MDSA. As a result, this research demonstrated ways to utilize the pressure gradient near the leading edge of a MDSA to counteract flow separation, and it provided insights that can be applied to improve MDSA designs for practical use. To explore the applicability of this knowledge to more complex geometries, a similar MDSA was tested on a model of an aircraft with a high aspect ratio wing, and the data from this test will be used in a future study. The findings of this research are relevant to MDSA designs in general, and they can be applied to other types of devices that produce a pressure gradient on the surface of a turbine or a blade, such as those produced by a rotating blade or a jet. The discovery of the secondary vortex induced by the pressure gradient near the leading edge of a MDSA is considered a novel contribution of this research, and it is believed to be generally applicable to flow interactions involving a pressure gradient on the surface of a turbine or a blade. Analyzing a large dataset of 144,000 Americans' written comments gathered through a national survey, researchers found a significant inconsistency between their self-reported positive attitudes and the actual sentiment expressed in their written responses.  When focusing on specific topics like immigration, healthcare, and the economy, similar inconsistencies were observed.   are inferred from their corresponding halos using a forward model, and then

  This process involves multiple components, including the effects of incomplete
  observations, systematic biases in galaxy identification, and the influence of
  extremely rare and luminous galaxies. Previous studies have examined these
  components individually, but a comprehensive analysis of the combined effect is
  yet to be seen. In the context of the BEAGLE code, we have investigated how
  these components interact with each other and the simulation data, specifically
  focusing on the behavior in relation to halo mass, galaxy mass, and observational
  limits. We have found that the relationship between galaxy mass and halo mass is
  significantly distorted by incomplete observations, particularly in regions with
  moderate to high galaxy formation rates. We have further discovered that the
  remaining components have a more minor impact on the observed galaxy population.
  As such, our research emphasizes the importance of accounting for the effects of
  observations on the galaxy-halo connection, particularly in areas with high
  galaxy formation rates, and encourages future work on the comprehensive
  analysis of galaxy populations. This analysis will be critical in evaluating the
  validity of simulation-based models of the galaxy-halo connection and their use
  in predicting the populations of rare and luminous galaxies.  Ultimately, our
  findings stress that the behavior of massive galaxies cannot be accurately
  captured through forward modeling without considering the limitations of
  observations. The code used in this research is publicly available at

transportation system application: target tracking on multiple surfaces with varying orientations using a single active acoustic transducer. This system can be invaluable in monitoring and managing traffic, as it enables authorities to keep tabs on key transportation infrastructure without causing distractions for drivers. Our research focuses on employing a single active acoustic transducer to pinpoint targets sounding a constant tone on multiple surfaces, like road markings, and determine their three-dimensional positions. To achieve this task, we developed a model of the acoustic transmission and reception process, accounting for factors like sound speed, temperature, air flow, and surface characteristics, which we tested both theoretically and experimentally. Using a single transducer to transmit and receive sounds, we overcame the common challenge of interference between transmission and reception. We further addressed the challenge of target localization with limited viewing angles in the absence of direct sounds. Our experimental results confirmed our model's accuracy and allowed us to estimate the positions of targets sounding a constant tone with varying frequencies. We demonstrated the capability of a single active acoustic transducer to track targets on multiple surfaces with varying orientations by analyzing the received sound signals directly. To take direct sounds into consideration, we developed a method to correct the sound speed based on the surface slope. We validated this method on artificial surfaces and verified its applicability to real-world surfaces. We also investigated different signal processing techniques to improve the accuracy of target position estimation. Our research on single active acoustic transducer target tracking has significant implications for intelligent transportation systems, as it provides a cost-effective and non-intrusive way to monitor traffic infrastructure without causing distractions for drivers.   traffic flow theory that represents the interaction between vehicles and roads.
  This model is particularly useful for analyzing and predicting traffic dynamics,
  especially in complex scenarios like merging lanes, intersections, and
  roundabouts. However, applying the tube method to these scenarios is challenging
  due to unknown values for certain parameters, which hinders its application in
  practice. This study addresses this limitation by developing a novel approach
  to calculate a crucial parameter in the volume-of-tube model, known as the
  effective tolerance, which is a measure of how closely vehicles can follow one
  another without slowing down. This study focuses on urban environments and
  proposes a method to estimate the effective tolerance based on the speed of the
  vehicles. It then applies this parameter to the volume-of-tube model in a
  practical scenario, analyzing the impact of vehicle closeness on driving speed.

  speeds in Japanese cities and includes features like road type and presence of
  turn lanes. It then uses machine learning techniques to predict the optimal

  finds that vehicles can travel even closer to each other, especially at lower
  speeds, and that the current Japanese speed limits are often set higher than

Our main conclusion is that the unstable manifold of a given semigroup can be related to the unstable manifold of its perturbed version for a significant period of time, even in the presence of time-varying components. This connection allows us to understand how small changes in age-structured systems affect their asymptotic behavior. Our approach involves using the characteristic equation associated with the semigroup's generator, the spectral mapping theorem, and the properties of non-autonomous dynamical systems to analyze the systems' asymptotic behavior. This research contributes an exponential attractor theory component to the study of non-autonomous parabolic equations and dynamical systems, in addition to providing a mathematical framework for understanding the stability of age-structured population dynamics systems and their generalizations. These studies have implications for modeling the spread of diseases within populations and other age-structured epidemiological models. 

  The stability of a stable non-autonomous semigroup of age-structured population dynamics systems with time-varying parameters can be determined by examining the characteristics of its generator, specifically the properties of its characteristic equation, which defines the behavior of the system's solutions. This approach allows us to extend the theory of invariant manifolds to non-autonomous systems and provides a framework for studying the spread of diseases and other age-structured epidemiological models. 

  Our findings also demonstrate that the asymptotic behavior of small perturbations in age-structured systems remains essentially the same for a significant period, which is characterized by the dimension of the system's unstable manifold. This insight is critical for modeling the spread of diseases, as it reveals that an increase in the system's unstable manifold could indicate a shift from a stable equilibrium to an unstable one, resulting in the rapid spread of the disease. 

  In conclusion, our research into the stability of a stable non-autonomous semigroup of age-structured population dynamics systems with time-varying parameters has implications for modeling the spread of diseases and other age-structured epidemiological models, in addition to extending the theory of invariant manifolds to non-autonomous systems and providing a framework for analyzing the characteristics of these systems' asymptotic behaviors. 

  The studies presented in this research have a broad application in modeling the dynamics of populations with time-varying components, such as the impact of changing environmental conditions, demographic changes, and the flow of individuals between different age groups, and can be further extended to account for spatial aspects and the flow of individuals

Building on these measures, we introduce the notion of a geometric version, characterized by the sum of the degrees of the polynomial's component equations in each variable. This approach enables us to characterize functions with a bounded level of complexity under Gr\"obner basis computations, specifically those requiring a high degree in any combination of variables.  Specifically, a function $f$ is considered complex to the power $d$ if, for any projective transformation, the transformed $f$ has a set of defining equations with variables' degrees summing to more than $d$.  This property can be seen as a variant of Castelnuovo's theorem, which counts the degrees of the defining equations for a given projective curve, but with a significant addition, as it does so for any projective transformation of the original curve.  Our measures also enable us to investigate the complexity of functions arising from another context, specifically hyperelliptic curves defined over a number field, as these curves can be represented as pairs of polynomials with specific properties.  Based on these measures, we establish a boundary for the level of complexity of hyperelliptic curves that can be covered by a particular type of algorithm, which involves another component beyond the usual one based on the total degree.  This new component, in turn, is governed by a measure characterized by the sum of the degrees of the polynomial's component equations in each variable.  This insight allows us to create a more refined categorization of hyperelliptic curves and propose a computational approach tailored to those with a particular level of complexity.  As an example, we outline a step-by-step strategy for finding the rational points of a specific type of hyperelliptic curve, which serves as an instance of the algorithmic problem we are addressing.  This strategy is based on a combination of mathematical developments and an initial point, from which the algorithm can iterate.  This strategy is applicable to curves with a specific level of complexity and can be computationally demanding, but it is still an illustrative case of how such curves can be covered by an algorithm. This research focused on analyzing discharge-related fluctuations in low-density solar wind conditions, specifically assessing the effectiveness of a simple model attributing these fluctuations to the interaction between the spacecraft and the local plasma. The model, which depends on the sheath around the spacecraft, was tested against FPF data from the pre-solar array in low-power modes. Our findings confirm previous results and provide more detailed evidence that the fluctuations behave as expected when the spacecraft potential becomes negative, as predicted by the model. However, we also observed discrepancies between the measured and predicted fluctuations when the spacecraft potential remains positive, which cannot be explained by the current model. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the fluctuations correlate with each other in both cases, as predicted by the model, but this correlation becomes stronger when the fluctuations are larger (i.e., more negative potentials) and occurs more frequently when the solar wind speed is slower. This supports previous interpretations and suggests that slower solar winds lead to more negative potentials and larger fluctuations more often, as if they were pushing the spacecraft potential over the threshold more frequently. This research highlights the limitations of the current model and the need for a more comprehensive understanding of the discharge processes and the effects of solar wind conditions on the fluctuations. This understanding is crucial for accurately interpreting measurements of the floating potential and the effects of space environment on spacecraft in similar configurations. The analysis of the discharge-related fluctuations in the FPF data cannot be applied to high-density environments found near comets, but to low-density solar wind conditions encountered during the Rosetta mission outside of 1.7 AU from the Sun. Despite significant advances in modeling and data collection, the, so-called initial value problem for the climate system remains unresolved. In contrast, the influence of initial conditions on the climate system's response to external forcing, the, so-called initial condition problem, has not received sufficient attention. This study investigates how the climate system responds to external forcing in the, so-called energy space, and reveals that it acts as a filter that amplifies certain patterns of energy, while reducing others. Furthermore, we discovered that the climate system's response to asymmetric solar variability, as seen during the, Holocene solar minimum, can result in the amplification of specific modes of variability, such as the El Nio Southern Oscillation, and may have contributed to the increased frequency of extreme El Nino events during that period. We investigate the expectation of the number of vertices, edges, and 2-simplices in a random 2-dimensional complex, and establish that this expectation behaves like a translation-invariant measure for the linear order space. We also examine the case where the linear order space is the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and show that the expectation of the number of vertices, edges, and 2-simplices in a random 2-dimensional complex for this space grows as $O(n^d)$, where $n$ is the number of vertices. Our findings significantly improve previous work by Aleshahin and Miller, and provide a more precise understanding of the structure of random 2-dimensional complexes in these spaces. Our approach to studying these complexes involves combinatorial and geometric analysis, and may be seen as an initial exploration of the broader topic of translating invariant measures for geodesic graphs.   a peer-to-peer network and IoT technology to detect and prevent cyber attacks,
  and incorporates a blockchain-based mechanism to protect the network from
  malicious nodes and unauthorized changes. Furthermore, NEST features a
  self-healing capability that detects and isolates compromised devices within the
  network. Our approach has the added benefit of simplifying future system
  expansions and upgrades. We have implemented a prototype of NEST using the

  individual devices. Our findings demonstrate that NEST achieves high levels of

This quantum version achieves an exponential speedup compared to its classical counterpart, specifically a $2^{n/2 - o(n)}$ increase in the length of the shortest vector, where $n$ represents the dimension of the lattice. Furthermore, this quantum algorithm exhibits a time complexity of $L^{2.5} poly(n, log(L))$, a quantity that indicates its efficiency for large lattice dimensions, and a space complexity of $poly(log(L), n)$, indicating its memory requirements. This new algorithm holds promise for applying lattice reduction in problem-solving scenarios. To evaluate its efficacy, we examined several scenarios and found that for a significant range of lattice dimensions, a quantum computer could determine whether a lattice contains a vector of a particular length, a capability that exceeds the capabilities of its classical counterpart.

  We also developed an alternative version of the Helfgott algorithm that employs a distinct approach and potentially more substantial speedups for particular lattice dimensions, although this version is not suitable for a quantum implementation. 

  We highlight the key components of the Helfgott algorithm and discuss the role of its parameters for context.

Specifically, we show how to compute the least labelled abstract state for a safety automaton, and demonstrate this is equivalent to finding the smallest subset of states requiring infinite exploration in an infinite run. To achieve this, we introduce a more general concept, the minimum model for a safety automaton defined by a property P, which we further characterise as the smallest transitive closure of a set of states that satisfy P. We implement these models using a novel representation of transitive closure, a compact matrix format that reduces complex operations on closure to simple matrix multiplications, and includes efficient detection of closure for specific state configurations. Our approach is adaptable and provides a universal framework for modelling safety properties, which we support with an in-depth analysis of its computational advantages and disadvantages. Moreover, we make our implementation publicly available under an open-source licence. Our results are validated through experimental data from testing our approach on a variety of benchmarks and scenarios. Our research on safety property models also gives us insights that are applicable to other settings, such as the recent challenge of minimising recursive abstractions in universal automata.   an average 35% reduction in power consumption in various computational

  is particularly beneficial for applications with high memory access patterns.

  memory access, including adjusting data placement, read/write access speeds,

  environment to facilitate the development and testing of energy-efficient memory

  patterns and those that are memory-bound.

Specifically, we examine the implications of a variation of a theorem of Shih, which states that under certain conditions, a subgroup of a residually finite group with a specific property is itself residually finite.  This variant has more general applications than the original theorem.  We also discuss other developments in this area of study.  These discussions build on the findings presented at the 2017 Galway conference on finite groups.  We highlight the key results from the papers of our colleagues, particularly those of Cornuel's theorem variants, the compatibility of certain properties with finite images, and the connections between finiteness and residual finiteness.  We also examine the group $E_{431}$ of automorphisms of a free group of finite rank, the group $Aut_F(G)$ of automorphisms of a group $G$ that fix a specific free subgroup, and the group $R_c$ of automorphisms that preserve a collection of conjugacy classes.  We discuss the residuality of these groups and explore the broader context of our discussions, which are centered on the fundamental question of when a property is inherited by subgroups from its parent group.  We emphasize that the discussions of certain examples are based on the calculations of our colleagues, which we present in a simplified form to highlight the key features of these examples.  We note that some of these discussions are also related to the commutativity of certain subgroups and the compatibility of properties with finite images, which are important topics in their own right.   times between different pairs of players, what information is shared and how it is

  among groups. The results show that shorter memory lengths lead to more cooperation

Real-time communications within packet-switched networks heavily depend on  
the resource reservation protocol, RSVP, to deliver data packets in a timely manner.  
Despite its importance, RSVP's reliability and efficiency have been subject to scrutiny  
due to its inherent flaws, particularly the absence of timely feedback mechanisms  
and the substantial amount of control traffic it generates. Our research explores a  
more efficient approach to providing real-time services over IP networks, utilizing  
existing infrastructure and services with a focus on timely feedback and low overhead.  
This approach is compared to the traditional RSVP method and promising results  
justify its potential as a viable alternative. Our findings also serve as a base  
to further improve this method with a focus on integrating it into existing IP  
infrastructure. Our research explicitly addresses issues such as delay estimation,  
efficient reservation strategies, and the impact of existing services on IP networks,  
and we present a scalable architecture to support real-time services with a focus  
on timely feedback and low overhead. Our results demonstrate improved performance  
indicators, including smaller delay peaks and jitters, which further support the  
potential of this method as a viable alternative to traditional RSVP methods.  
Our research on this topic is ongoing and we welcome any feedback, especially  
from the research community, to further refine this method. This research was  
presented at the 2003 IEEE Wireless Communications and Networking Conference.  
Our findings also justify the necessity to enhance existing IP services with  
timely feedback mechanisms to ensure efficient and reliable real-time communications  
over IP networks. Our approach to providing real-time services over IP networks  
has several benefits, including low overhead, efficient delay estimation,  
and the ability to adapt to varying network conditions, and it supports a wide  
range of real-time applications, including voice, video, and online games.  
Our results demonstrate that this approach yields substantial improvements in  
indicators of performance, including smaller delay peaks and jitters, and it  
experiences significantly less packet loss and retransmissions, which further  
support its potential as a viable alternative to traditional methods.

a single introduction in a fully mixed population over time can be represented by a reproductive ratio, $R(t)$. In the context of infectious diseases, $R(t)$ indicates the number of people an infected individual will go on to infect on average at time $t$. The course of an epidemic is ultimately determined by the relationship between $R(t)$ and $t$, and is influenced by factors such as virus transmission speed and immunity development rate. This paper focuses on analyzing the connection between $R(t)$ and the epidemic trajectory, especially in populations where interactions remain consistent over time, known as confiding networks. Our study examines how the shape of $R(t)$ changes in these networks and its impact on epidemic outcomes. We also investigate the integral of $R(t)$ across the entire duration of an epidemic and derive an equation that relates this integral to the final epidemic size. Our results can be applied to modeling various infectious diseases, including COVID-19, influenza, and measles. Our study reveals that the traditional reproductive ratio, $R_0$, which is the value of $R(t)$ at time $t=0$, does not adequately capture the complexity of epidemic dynamics and can lead to inaccurate predictions if it varies throughout the epidemic. This occurs because $R_0$ fails to account for introduced infections that occur after the initial stage of the epidemic. We emphasize the importance of considering $R(t)$ in its entirety to accurately predict the future course of an epidemic. This can be achieved by modeling the shape of $R(t)$ and integrating it over time. Our results also highlight the significance of certain epidemiological parameters, such as the virus transmission speed and immunity development rate, in influencing the shape of $R(t)$. We validate our model predictions using empirical data from simulated and actual epidemics, including the 1918 Spanish Flu pandemic and the recent COVID-19 outbreak in Wuhan, China. Our research underscores that studying $R(t)$ is crucial for accurately predicting the future trajectory of an epidemic and determining the effectiveness of control measures being implemented. This is because the relationship between $R(t)$ and the epidemic trajectory determines the outcomes of these measures. Our findings also provide insights into the behavior of $R(t)$ in different stages of an epidemic, which can help in evaluating and optimizing control strategies. We demonstrate that implementing control measures can alter the shape of $R(t)$, and thereby influence the epidemic trajectory. This occurs because the time it takes for introduced infections to manifest as new cases is longer in populations with dense confiding networks.

This model enables the inclusion of a chiral symmetry breaking complex scalar field and random domain wall effects to directly influence the surface band structure. Initially, we will cover the fundamentals of large $N$ limits in various contexts, including classical and quantum field theories, string theories, and statistical models.  Next, we will delve into the properties and applications of the Yang-Baxter algebra, which is a fundamental structure underlying many complex systems.  Specifically, we will examine its appearances in quantum groups, conformal field theories, topological insulators, and scattering theories.  Along the way, we will also explore the relationships between the Yang-Baxter algebra and 2-cocycles, bialgebras, coboundary objects, and symmetric matrices.  Building on the introductory material, we will delve into more advanced topics, including a proposed formulation of quantum mechanics, a look at the fundamental principles underlying the Yang-Baxter algebra, and a discussion of its connections to 2-cocycles and bialgebras.  Finally, we will conclude by connecting the Yang-Baxter algebra to symplectic and Poisson structures, Lie algebras, and integrable systems.  This summary provides a high-level overview of the complex and interconnected topics covered in these lectures.  A brief introduction sets the stage for our exploration of large $N$ limits and the Yang-Baxter algebra.  The next several sections lay the foundations for the Yang-Baxter algebra, beginning with its basic properties and examples, followed by an examination of its appearances in physics and mathematics.  We then delve deeper into the algebra's structure, exploring its relationships to quantum groups, conformal field theories, topological insulators, and scattering theories.  In the second part of our discussion, we explore more advanced topics, starting with a proposed formulation of quantum mechanics and a look at the fundamental principles underlying the Yang-Baxter algebra.  We also examine its connections to 2-cocycles, bialgebras, coboundary objects, and symmetric matrices.  Finally, we discuss the Yang-Baxter algebra's connections to symplectic and Poisson structures, Lie algebras, and integrable systems.  Our conclusion highlights the complex and interconnected nature of these topics and the many open questions and areas for further research.  A comprehensive bibliography is included to aid in exploring these topics in greater depth.   spike protein to understand its interaction with water and oxygen through 
  first-principles calculations. The results reveal that the oxygen atoms bonded 
  to the hydroxyl groups of the spike protein exhibit a significant shift in 
  electron density, suggesting they may act as lone pairs that form pi bonds 
  with delocalized electrons from the phenyl groups, potentially facilitating 
  protein-water and protein-oxygen interactions. Notably, the presence of these 
  lone pairs may also make the bound oxygen atoms more accessible to oxygen 
  molecules, paving the way for a new understanding of the virus-oxygen 
  interaction that could influence the transmission and binding of the virus 
  to host cells. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for experimental and 
  biochemical studies on the spike protein and suggest that the oxygen atoms 
  bonded to the hydroxyl groups may serve as key sites for future anti-SARS-

  lone pairs into models of the spike protein, particularly when simulating 
  water and oxygen interactions, and can serve as a reference for future

In this research, we explore the potential for a related language to act as a resource language to facilitate the development of a model for an unrelated language, leveraging the presence of parallel text data. Applying this theory to one-dimensional maps, we can examine the structural aspects that underpin the generation of chaos, particularly in systems characterized by unimodal dynamics. Our investigation focuses on the 1-dimensional Henon map, a standard model of chaos, and uses the Koopman operator to uncover the underlying, globally defined dynamics. By analyzing the operator's invariant structures, we uncovered the source of chaos in the Henon map: it results from a non-trivial, higher-dimensional invariant set, formed by a combination of a unstable fixed point and an unstable periodic orbit: this finding contrasts with the traditional view that chaos arises from the expansion of a single fixed point. This discovery suggests that, in the unimodal context, chaos emerges when the internal reflection of the dynamics, resulting from the interaction between the system's dynamics and its own topological obstacles, becomes an internal source of noise that generates local, seemingly random behavior. This research offers a quantitative explanation for the Henon map's chaos and demonstrates the power of Koopman operator theory in uncovering the underlying, globally defined dynamics that give rise to local, seemingly random behavior in dynamical systems. This approach can be applied to a wide range of unimodal maps and other types of nonlinear systems, including the logistic map, the complex Henon map, and the Quasi-Periodic Schr\"{o}dinger equation. This research also highlights the connection between the Koopman operator's invariant structures and the characterstic patterns of chaos in unimodal dynamics, and provides a precise, operator-based definition of chaos. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach is compatible with numerical methods, such as nonlinear dynamics and machine learning, and provide a case study on the prediction of rational approximation gaps in quasi-periodic signals using a nonlinear autoregressive model. Our work builds upon the existing research of Knuth, who identified ordered trees according to their leaf counts and distinguished them from root-free trees, which he called "free trees." We demonstrate that free trees correspond to the class of ordered trees with a maximum depth of one, equivalent to linearly ordered sets of two elements. This research is accompanied by formal definitions and specified patterns of avoided subtrees. This research is supported by the theory of forbidden patterns of subtrees, which also enables the computation of certain enumerative properties of these tree classes. We also touch upon the Dyck paths, which arise from the first-order formulation of tree properties and offer an independent line of inquiry. a disordered to an ordered environment. Through direct measurements of noise in
in-situ experiments and numerical simulations of the full many-body system, we found
that this change causes a permanent increase in momentum fluctuations, leading to
a population of solitary waves that propagate at a constant speed. Our results
also reveal that this behavior is linked to a stoichiometric instability, with the
gas attempting to return to a state of equilibrium through the generation of
excitations similar to the Korteweg-de Vries breather. Our research demonstrated
experimentally the existence of the Korteweg-de Vries breather and provided clear
explanations for the noise characteristics, the stability of the solitary waves, and
the formation of ring structures that form as a result of this process. Our study
has far-reaching implications for our understanding of self-organization in matter,
as well as for the development of models for high-dimensional scenarios and two-
dimensional systems. Our work also highlights the usefulness of noise measurements
in assessing the stability of low-dimensional systems and suggests possible routes
for observing the Korteweg-de Vries breather in other settings. Overall, our study

We propose testing the LISA sensitivity to magnetic fields in low-mass black hole binaries, taking into account their influence on gravitational waves via the magnetic stress mechanism.  By simulating a range of binary systems and analyzing the extracted signals, we identified the most promising targets and predicted the threshold values magnetic fields must exceed to affect LISA measurements.  Our study focuses on two models describing the accretion disk behavior, specifically the Bardeen-Petterson disk and the slimmer, hot inner disk, each yielding distinct predictions for gravitational waves.  Ultimately, our findings suggest that LISA can measure magnetic fields in the range of $10^{4}-10^{5}$ G within the binary system, offering a direct assessment of this key parameter through the analysis of measured gravitational waves.  This assessment is made possible by incorporating the effects of magnetic fields into the analysis of GW190521, the most massive binary black hole merger detected to date, and observing that even at this high merger rate, magnetic fields cannot exceed $10^{5}$ G.  This prediction will be continuously refined as more information becomes available from future mergers.  This assessment is further supported by the analysis of a large population of binary black hole mergers, including both massive and intermediate-mass combinations, and our results indicate that LISA will be capable of determining the effects of magnetic fields in the range of $10^{4}-10^{5}$ G with approximately 90\% confidence in its early operating years.  This prediction is derived from the analysis of GW190521 and other mergers, specifically the heavy black hole mergers S200606939 and S200626759, with total masses of 93.2 M_\odot and 63.5 M_\odot respectively, and our study confirms that magnetic fields in the range of $10^{4}-10^{5}$ G cannot explain the slight deviations from general relativity in these events.  This prediction will continuously refine as more information becomes available from future mergers.  We further emphasize that the effects of magnetic fields on gravitational waves are influenced by the angle at which they interact with the accretion disk, specifically the innermost, hot, slim disk, and our study indicates that the stress mechanism is more pronounced in binary systems with masses in the range of 5-30 M_\odot. One type of monoidal functor of this kind is called a strong functor, and when this functor is part of a larger structure, it's known as a strong transformation within a context.   different approaches on the same group of students: a pure procedural one and 
  a object-oriented one. The assessment method employed identical, challenging 
  trials before and after the courses to evaluate the students' learning results 
  and curve fitting skills. The main findings show that, despite the potential 
  difficulties of object-Oriented Programming, beginners can write efficient programs 
  using objects just as well as with a procedural approach. In fact, there was 
  no noticeable disadvantage in using objects right from the start. These results 
  contradict the common assumption that new programmers need a procedural 
  introduction to programming. The same data revealed a significant improvement 
  in both curricula in the second trial, indicating a decrease in students' 
  frustration as they gained experience. The most successful students, as assessed 
  by the automated grader, used both curricula with equal frequency. The 
  overall assessment indicates that starting with a procedural approach does not 
  provide a significant advantage for beginners, and object-Oriented Programming 
  is not more difficult for them than a procedural one.

The first group consists of casual observers who vote based on their current knowledge, while the second group includes more informed voters who consider their past knowledge in their decision-making process. We examine the impact of these different voting strategies on the overall social choice, specifically how they affect coordination and efficiency. The model allows us to analyze several scenarios: one in which both groups of voters make informed decisions, a scenario where only the more informed voters make informed choices, and a scenario where neither group makes informed choices. We also consider various relationships between the individual and social optima and investigate how the two types of voters coordinate their votes with each other. We demonstrate that in certain conditions, voting can lead to the social optimum, though this is not always the case, especially when the groups have different levels of trust in each other's knowledge and preferences. We utilize a novel approach based on learning equilibria to understand the dynamics of voting in this model, highlighting the significance of "learning from experience" in achieving social efficiency. We propose distinguishing between two types of casual observations: new information that reveals previously unknown knowledge and a repetition of already known information. We then explore the implications of each type of observation on the social choice and learning process. We also investigate how the presence of both types of voters can lead to a mutually beneficial exchange of knowledge, facilitating more efficient social choices. We emphasize the crucial role that trust plays in this exchange, as over-trust can result in undesirable consequences, including less efficient choices and even social dilemmas. We conclude by discussing the applicability of this model to various real-world settings, such as business, social, and sporting contexts, and suggest potential modifications to the model, including adding multiple casual observer groups and introducing reputation systems. We also examine the connection between this model and existing literature on learning dynamics, mutual knowledge, and common knowledge, as well as the potential benefits of reciprocity and trust-based learning equilibria. This limitation is particularly pronounced in the domain of descriptive text, which is characterized by a high degree of noise. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach, NoLook, that leverages descriptive text for supervised learning. NoLook employs a strategic mixture of clean and noisy data to train a model. When using clean data, the model focuses on precise representations, and when using noisy data, the model prioritizes robust representations. This distinction is achieved through a dynamic attention mechanism that adapts to the nature of the input data. Furthermore, NoLook incorporates a feature reinforcement module to emphasize crucial text descriptors. Our experiments demonstrate that NoLook yields substantial improvements over pre-trained language models in various supervised learning tasks, especially those involving descriptive text. This improvement is evident across different noise levels and data sets, showcasing the versatility of our proposed approach. Code for NoLook is available at https://github.com/ghrua/nolook.  Pre-trained language models have achieved notable success across a broad spectrum of natural language processing tasks. However, their performance significantly declines when processing noisy data, particularly when describing complex scenes. To address this limitation, we introduce the NovelLook model, which utilizes descriptive text for supervised learning. NovelLook employs a strategic blend of clean and noisy data to train the model. When using clean data, the model focuses on precise visual representations, while using noisy data leads to more robust representations. This distinction is achieved through a dynamic attention mechanism that adapts to the nature of the input data. Furthermore, NovelLook incorporates a feature reinforcement module to emphasize crucial text descriptors. Our findings reveal that NovelLook yields substantial improvements over pre-trained language models in various supervised learning tasks, especially those involving descriptive text. This improvement is evident across different noise levels and data sets, showcasing the versatility of our proposed approach. Code for NovelLook is available at https://github.com/ghrua/nolook.  The NovelLook model exhibits notable visual understanding when describing simple scenes. To further enhance its visual understanding, we introduce the NovelLook-VIS model, which incorporates visual information into the descriptive text. NovelLook-VIS leverages the section and phrase structures of descriptive text to guide the attention of the visual model, while the visual model informs the feature reinforcement module to emphasize crucial visual elements. Perot cavity is highly sensitive to tiny changes in its length, making it extremely effective in detecting minor displacements.  Using a well-controlled laser, we measured the amplitude of fluctuations in optical phase space to derive details about the cavity's length variations and surrounding environmental influences.  Conducting these measurements in various environmental conditions, we found that movements of the air around the cavity and its attachment to the table caused more significant phase fluctuations than vibrations of the table itself or acoustic noise.  We demonstrated that, in optimal conditions, a cavity with a 1 km optical length can detect displacements as minor as 4.5 x 10^-12, which is equivalent to a length change of approximately 0.25 pm, and this detection capability can be improved further by utilizing higher finesse cavities.  In addition to its applications in sensing technology, a cavity with similar properties is also highly suitable for generating Squeezed light in Optomechanical systems.  We developed an analytical model for describing the dynamics of light that has undergone Squeezing, and our findings confirmed previous insights into the relationship between Squeezing and photon loss.  We also found that the degree of Squeezing is influenced by the strength of laser power and the type of mirror used, and our predictions for generating large amounts of Squeezed light are based on calculating the optimal parameters for 100 dB Squeezing, which is equivalent to reducing the photon noise by two orders of magnitude, and this can be achieved with a 10 km cavity that has a 10 million finesse and produces 1 W of Squeezed light.  We believe that our model is highly versatile and can be applied to various configurations of Optomechanical systems that generate Squeezed light for a wide range of applications, including high-precision measurements in Metrology, Gravitational Wave detection in LIGO, and developing sensitive navigation systems for GPS.  We also discussed the potential for utilizing large, high-finesse cavities in a setup for generating Squeezed light that is correlated with mechanical vibrations at the mirror, and our predictions indicate that this setup is capable of generating 100 dB Squeezing while detecting displacements as minor as 10^-9, which is equivalent to a length change of approximately 50 pm, and this detection capability can be improved further by utilizing a cavity with an optical length of 100 km. The energy-independent signals with low frequencies in the spectrum of IGR J12583-019 and XTE J15560-6648 suggest that these sources are characterized by a unique type of quasiperiodic variability, potentially linked to a turbulent accretion flow in their systems. We examine the ordered eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of these graphs and characterize their asymptotic behavior for $n$ varying widely (powers of two for simplicity). Our main finding involves defining a natural timescale for the eigenvalue distribution based on the logarithm of the number of vertices and demonstrating that the eigenvalue sequence exhibits distinct behavior on each timescale. Our research also incorporates the application of multiple scaling factors to further illustrate the asymptotic properties of these eigenvalues. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of these random graphs exhibit a phase transition, with their behavior changing fundamentally as the grid becomes interconnected enough to form a single component. Our results also provide a framework for comparing our findings to other models of random graphs, such as the Erdos-Renyi model, which are characterized by a different type of connectivity structure. Our research methodology leverages a novel combination of traditional mathematical eigenvalue analysis techniques with modern empirical findings derived from extensive numerical matrix calculations. Our data involves the computation of hundreds of thousands of eigenvalues of large, sparse matrices representing the adjacency relationships of highly complex grid structures. Our findings have implications for understanding the fundamental properties of random graphs and their matrix representations and also provide a foundation for exploring the asymptotic properties of other complex, interconnected systems. Our research reveals that the eigenvalues of these random graphs exhibit a phase transition as the connection density increases, with the distribution of their values becoming increasingly diverse across different timescales as the graphs become more interconnected. Our analysis also highlights the significance of the grid's connectivity component, particularly the largest connected component, in determining the structure of the matrix and, by extension, the eigenvalues. Our results demonstrate that the eigenvalues of these random graphs reflect their connectedness structure, with the appearance of multiple distinct submatrices corresponding to the connected components of the graph. Our research also involves the introduction of a new connected component-specific timescale for each component of the graph and reveals that the eigenvalues exhibit a tendency to cluster together on each of these timescales. Our findings also provide a framework for generalizing our results to account for the effects of different connection densities across the graph's components. This research focuses on assessing the effectiveness of performance, behavior, and collaboration features in determining individual student knowledge through the lens of critical discourse analysis.  Although previous studies have examined the relationship between student knowledge and learning behaviors, this research delves deeper into the underlying meanings of learning interactions.  Using a theoretical framework based on Vygotsky's concept of the "higher mental functions," we analyze the ways students construct knowledge through social learning interactions.  Our findings indicate that performance and behavior indicators reflect students' applied knowledge, while collaboration indicators reveal their capacity for metacognition.  We contend that performance, behavior, and collaboration measures can predict student knowledge, though the accuracy of these predictions is influenced by the presence of metacognitive dialogue in learning interactions.  We propose that future research consider the role of metacognition in promoting higher mental functions and integrating explicit and implicit knowledge.  As such, we suggest re-examining the sequence of learning interactions as presented in our case study, and exploring the connection between students' critical discourse and their constructed knowledge. The observation of 3C 29, a system comprising a star with a neutron star or black hole orbiting a massive companion, has been observed across the electromagnetic spectrum, including visible, X-ray and gamma-ray wavelengths. Although it was initially noted in the 1990s, 3C 29 didn't gain significant attention until the detection of its gamma-ray emissions in 2019 through the Fermi-LAT.   optimizing computer instructions for better performance on specific workloads. 
  This technique contrasts with conventional, broader-minded processor design approaches.
  In this research, we apply instruction tuning to address two pressing issues facing 
  modern computing: power consumption and security risks resulting from side-channel attacks.
  First, we develop new instructions to minimize the energy expenditure of two widely 
  used memory access operations, leading to a 30-50 percent reduction in power usage 
  for certain memory-intensive applications.

  benchmark suite consisting of real-world applications.
  We further investigate how a tuning environment can be optimized to prioritize 
  performance, area usage, and power consumption when developing tailored computer 
  instructions, proposing a simple, programmable matrix-based approach to achieve 
  balanced design results.
  Finally, we highlight the potential challenges and potential solutions for integrating 
  tailored computer instructions into practical processor designs.

  demonstrate the diverse distributions of gas that can result from varying rotation

Specifically, for a group G that is classical and has high rank, we establish the existence of a maximal subgroup of specific type within G, characterized by its relatively small size and inclusion in a parabolic subgroup of G. This achievement is made possible by our analysis of highly soluble 2-local subgroups of G, which enables us to identify maximal subgroups of G that are dependent on its 2-rank. In addition, we obtain detailed information regarding these maximal subgroups, including their faithful complex irreducible characters and their associated monomial permutations. Furthermore, we develop a characterization of maximal subgroups of simple groups of exceptional Lie type, building on our earlier findings in [21]. A significant aspect of our findings is the definition of a new family, referred to as C-Subgroups, which encompasses maximal subgroups of a specific type and provides a crucial contribution to the description of the 2-local structure of a finite simple group of exceptional Lie type. A particular consequence of our characterisation is the derivation of new information regarding the Glaisher invariants of a finite simple group of exceptional Lie type, which, together with our earlier results in [21], enables us to determine the Glaisher invariants of nearly all finite simple groups of non-trivial classification. A notable exception remains for certain groups of large characteristic, which, as noted in [21], are associated with the Chevalley groups $^{2}G_{2}(3^{1/2})$ and $^{2}A_{l}(3^{1/2})$. A key aspect of our characterisation is the identification of a maximal subgroup of type SU(3) within a Chevalley group $^{2}A_{l}(3^{1/2})$, which, to the best of our knowledge, represents a novel discovery. This context involves a one-player game, specifically the kind that requires a verification procedure to validate moves, and the kind of strategy required to win such a game.  We show that a particular type of one-player game, one with a verification procedure that checks the satisfaction of norms, has games associated with it that are equivalent to problems already known to be of varying complexity. This hierarchy has a key property where each step can be determined in a linear time that increases with each level.  We demonstrate that this property is the key characteristic that defines polynomial time complexity, and that it can be used to create games of any desired polynomial time complexity.
